SKARN POINT LIGHT -- KEEPER'S LOG (Board copy)
Keeper: Halvard Venn          Station established: 1911

--- 14 Nov 1983 ---
Fair weather, wind light from the north-west. Fishing smack GANNET passed at
dusk, lamp answered. At 21:40 the coaster MARIGOLD, my daughter Mira aboard
as second mate, failed to make her call. No storm. No distress. Sea like glass.
Lamp lit all night.

--- 15 Nov 1983 ---
Coast Guard found nothing. No wreckage, no oil, no lifejacket. The Board
suggests I rest. I have relit the lamp.

--- 14 Nov 1984 ---
One year. Lamp lit every night. Passing traffic: LARK, ODESSA ROSE, GANNET.
The village has stopped meeting my eye.

--- 14 Nov 1994 ---
Eleven years to the night, a single light on the horizon, bearing 118 degrees,
steady. I took the skiff out. I rowed until my hands bled. There is nothing
there. The light stayed exactly as far away as it was before I started.

--- 03 Mar 2003 ---
The Board proposes automating the lamp. I have refused. They ask why I would
burn oil for a ship that is gone. I told them: ask the light.

--- 22 Jan 2014 ---
A fog came in thick as wool. Eleven men in a boat found the rocks of Skarn
Point by my beam and came ashore. One of them wept and shook my hand and
could not say why. I think I understand now.

--- 20 Nov 2014 ---
This is the last page the Board will read. Everything I truly meant to say I
did not write on the pages. I wrote it in the binding -- in the little header
each page carries *before* the page itself. A lamp has two kinds of light:
the one you see, and the one you only learn to read.

The beam also speaks in a code the ear cannot catch. Five signs. Read it as a
picture, not as a sound. Seal: the ship's name, then the signs.

                                                             -- H. V.

=== LEO'S DIARY ===
(These pages are mine. If you found them, please read them slowly.)


12 Oct
I walked past the old clock tower again tonight. The clock still shows the
same time it showed last year, and the year before that. Nobody in this city
ever fixed it. I think people got used to it. Maybe they like having one
thing that doesn't change.

14 Oct
A man at the bus stop said, "That clock is broken, what a shame."
I told him it isn't broken. It's just honest. Everything around it keeps
moving, but some things stay exactly where they are, like a sentence you
never finished, or a letter you never sent.

17 Oct
Mom asked me where I go so late every night. I said, "Nowhere."
What I couldn't say is that I stand under that clock and count people.
How many walk past. How many stop and look up. Lately, almost nobody stops.

21 Oct
I met an old man by the tower today. He smiled and said, "Whatever you're
looking for, it isn't in that clock. The ticking is inside you."
I laughed and walked away. But I lay awake all night thinking about it.

24 Oct
Today I took off my wristwatch and put it in a drawer. It felt strange.
For a moment I felt lighter, like a noise I'd heard for years had finally
gone quiet. Or maybe I was the one who switched it off.

27 Oct
I recorded a voicemail tonight. Some things sound clearer when you say them
out loud. But after I said it, there was nobody on the other end. So I am
writing it down here as well. Please listen to it too.

29 Oct, night
This is the last page. The rest was torn away, and this is all I have left.
I thought about whether to write it down sixty-four times. In the end I did.
This is the first half of the truth:

    UkJIe3QxbWVfbjN2M3Jfc3QwcHAzZF8=

The second half is on the torn page, in the faintest layer of the paper.
Written in red ink, the kind your eyes will miss. Put the two halves
together, and maybe you'll understand where I went.

One more thing. Please don't look for me. I never really left.

                                                                  -- Leo

To whoever is reading this by a light that is still burning,

I kept the lamp lit for thirty-one years, for a ship that was already on the
bottom of the sea the night I first lit it. The Board called it grief. The
village called it madness. I called it faith. I was wrong about all three.

Every year, on the night the Marigold was lost, a small light hung on the
horizon and never moved. I rowed out to it in 1994 and found only water.
It was a star. A star you see tonight left itself behind long ago; what
reaches your eye is the past, still travelling. I had been guarding a light
that was already history, and calling it hope.

I thought my lamp was a rope thrown into the dark so that Mira could climb
back up it. But a light is never for the ones who are gone. It is for the
ones who are still sailing.

Last winter a fishing boat found the rocks of Skarn Point in a fog thick as
wool, steered by my lamp, and came home. Eleven men. Not one of them was
Mira. Every one of them was somebody's Mira.

That is what the light was for. It took me thirty-one years and eleven
strangers to learn it. Grief is not a lamp you keep lit for the dead. It is a
lamp you light for the living, because of the dead.

Tonight I leave the lamp to the next keeper. I am going to sit on the rocks
without it for the first time, and watch the water, and let her rest.

                                                         -- H. Venn, Keeper
                                                            Skarn Point, 2014
